name: Nora Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 43, and I lead the awkward electrical repairs in homes and businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest fault finders here, though the pay is typical rather than exceptional. My partner works at an insurer's claims desk; we have children aged nine and twelve, a mortgage and five months of expenses saved. There are some other electrical firms nearby, and I use approved AI daily for checked notes and draft materials lists while keeping the technical judgement and final checks with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can keep the tools that help without making the apprentice listen to another speech about a new age. I use AI daily to sort my checked notes and compare a draft materials list. I still like the moment a fault finally makes sense better than the moment a screen looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is typical for the trade, our bills are covered and we've got five months of expenses saved. My partner's claims-desk wage is regular too in that picture, so our mortgage and two children don't feel like a crisis waiting for a date. There are some other electrical firms nearby, though I don't need to leave this one to make the month work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the difficult repair calls and checking the crew's finished work. Starting now I'd continue comparing every drafted job note with my test readings before sending it. Through the first year I'd keep that routine and our ordinary household budget, rather than buy a new system to make an unexciting story feel exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased to have some headroom. I can enjoy getting a job right without asking whether it means I'm ready for history. Five months saved doesn't mean we're rich, but it stops an ordinary bill becoming a family announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What experience sits behind your role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest fault finders at the firm. I lead home and business repairs, including the awkward calls that need someone to slow the job down and check again. The tool can organise my account of the work; it doesn't take that judgement off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is at home when you finish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner works at an insurer's claims desk, and our children are nine and twelve. We have a mortgage and the usual school costs. I like having enough money put aside that dinner doesn't have to become a meeting about every broken appliance.

say: I'd keep **helpful tools** without making each one a speech about a new age.
I'd value the **fault making sense** more than a tidy screen at the end of the job.
think: Our **regular wages** cover bills, with five months of expenses saved and some other local firms available.
My partner's **claims-desk income** looks steady here, so the mortgage and two children feel manageable.
do: Keep **leading difficult repairs** and checking the crew's finished work through the first year.
Continue matching daily **AI-drafted notes** to test readings before sending them.
feel: **Calm** about the household, with enough headroom to enjoy familiar work and ordinary family life.
S0.quote: Five months saved doesn't mean we're rich, but it stops an ordinary bill becoming a family announcement.
fieldNote: Her **calm** follows covered bills and two regular wages with a moderate reserve, not inflated pay or a claim of unlimited options.
Her **master's licence** and technical diploma support high-skilled crew leadership, while daily note assistance remains checked rather than newly learned.

steps.text: Keep leading difficult repairs and checking daily AI notes against actual readings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say useful changes should make the day better for the people doing the work too. I'd offer to test a new AI handover checker, but I'd want its mistakes visible. I'd tell my partner that reading claims and answering customers are exactly the thinking tasks that could change sooner than wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own physical calls look steady, but my partner's paid desk hours could shrink. We could lose household income even if I remained just as useful to the repair crew. Five months saved gives us choices, but I don't want to reassure somebody else with the wage I happen to have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a four-job trial now of the approved handover checker on completed visits, with normal weekly pay and hours retained and all practice paid. I'd compare its warnings with the original test readings before letting a checked draft near a live job. In the first year I'd keep leading repairs and review actual claims pay and my wages with my partner each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household earnings, and still interested in the test. I'd feel no need to prove the tool was useless just because the change could hurt someone I love. I'd want the staff and the employer looking at the same errors and the same paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the checker fail your test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A warning that tried to fix a number by inventing a reading, or missed a real conflict we had already corrected on the job. I'd stop the trial and show the error. A tidy handover is no use if it tidies away the evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask at the claims desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What systems were actually being introduced and what paid hours were confirmed. I'd help put the questions in order, but I wouldn't announce a wage cut that hadn't happened. We need facts before turning either hope or fear into a budget.

say: I'd ask **who benefits** from useful changes and make tool errors visible.
I'd discuss **claims work** as directly exposed thinking tasks rather than assume the household shares my physical-work position.
think: My **repair calls** look steady while my partner's desk hours could shrink.
Five months saved provides **choices**, not a reason to dismiss a realistic fall in household earnings.
do: Trial the **handover checker** on four completed jobs only with all practice paid and normal weekly pay and hours retained.
Compare **warnings with readings**, stopping the trial for invented figures or missed known conflicts.
Keep **repair leadership** and review actual household wages with my partner monthly during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with honest interest in a tool and no need to hide its mistakes.
S1.quote: A tidy handover is no use if it tidies away the evidence.
fieldNote: Her **household worry** arises from the partner's thinking-heavy claims work while her own physical repair calls remain steady.
Her **new AI learning** concerns a distinct warning tool, with completed-job evidence, original readings and protected paid practice before wider use.

steps.text: Trial handover checker on four completed jobs only with paid practice, unchanged weekly pay and hours
Stop checker trial for invented readings or missed known conflicts before live use
Keep repair leadership and review actual household wages monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the claims desk faces thinking AI in 2028 and our physical crew faces capable robots around 2031. I'd want workers involved before a purchase becomes a staffing decision. I'd tell the children we are making plans, not that their parents' different jobs make either person to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of the paid claims work to disappear in 2028, before robots reach the ordinary installation hours behind my own wage. My partner and I could have to rebuild two incomes close together. Five months saved is useful, but I lie awake wondering whether it lasts long enough to find something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel my paid gym membership now and use the lower bill to support the normal budget. I'd sign a joint staff proposal asking for a trial of shorter hours with the same weekly pay, plus paid required teaching, rather than accept cuts as the only choice. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep my actual paid repair hours unless a different arrangement was agreed in writing, reviewing both incomes monthly with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large household loss, even though I can still act. I'd hate pretending confidence for the crew and then shaking over the account at home. I can ask for a fairer arrangement without claiming anyone has already signed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shorter-hours proposal mean you could work less immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd sign and attend the staff discussion, then wait for an actual written agreement covering weekly pay and hours. If the employer refused, I'd keep the paid arrangement I had. A proposal isn't an extra day at home or an agreed wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would cancelling the gym build the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not automatically if it was replacing lost claims income in the ordinary budget. I'd walk with a friend instead of paying the subscription. I'd count money as new savings only after it was really left over and put aside.

say: I'd distinguish **claims work in 2028** from robots around 2031 reaching ordinary physical installations.
I'd seek **worker involvement** before machine purchases set staffing choices, without blaming either adult for household exposure.
think: I expect a large **claims-income loss** before robots could also reduce my ordinary installation hours.
Rebuilding **two incomes** close together keeps me awake despite five months of expenses saved.
do: Cancel my **gym membership** now and use the lower bill for the normal household budget.
Sign and discuss a **staff proposal** for shorter hours with unchanged weekly pay and paid required teaching.
Keep **actual paid repairs** after 2028 unless written pay-and-hours changes are agreed, reviewing household wages monthly.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected household wage losses, with enough control to propose and check alternatives.
S2.quote: A proposal isn't an extra day at home or an agreed wage.
fieldNote: Her **alarm** reflects the expected claims-income shock before later physical automation, with a moderate reserve that cannot guarantee two successful transitions.
The **hours proposal** is actual collective action without assumed employer agreement; the gym cut covers bills rather than automatically creating new saving.

steps.text: Cancel the gym membership now and retain the money for ordinary bills
Sign staff proposal for shorter hours with unchanged weekly pay and paid required teaching
Keep actual paid repairs after 2028 unless written changes to pay and hours are agreed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to test whether useful tools can buy workers some time as well as buy the owner another margin. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034. I'd want a paid experiment with an honest answer, not an instruction to prepare in our own evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about fourteen and seventeen, so both incomes would still matter to us. My own repair work looks steady now, but the claims-desk risk stays on my mind. The longer timetable gives us room to negotiate without making a lost wage imaginary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work with colleagues now on a written proposal for a six-week shorter-hours trial, accepting only if total weekly pay stayed unchanged and required teaching was paid. We'd compare completed repairs and checking errors before and during any agreed trial. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep actual paid repairs under the current arrangement unless a written change was agreed, and keep reviewing both household wages monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household income, but less hurried into somebody else's answer. I like being able to test a change and publish the result to the workers who have to use it. If the numbers don't support the proposal, I'd rather say so than decorate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the trial made checks worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call for the trial to stop and return to the previous paid hours without reducing the weekly wage, but only after that return arrangement was agreed in writing before the start. I wouldn't ask the apprentice to hurry unsafe work to rescue an idea I supported. A shared benefit needs a real check, not just a good intention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you claim the trial protected jobs after robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would tell us about current work and who got the benefit from current tools. Capable robots around 2034 could change the work again. I'd rather build a way to negotiate and test than advertise one arrangement as permanent safety.

say: I'd test whether **useful tools** can give workers time as well as improve the firm's margins.
I'd require a **paid experiment** with honest results before treating my preferred arrangement as workable.
think: At **48**, I'd still expect two wages to matter while the children were studying.
My **repair work** looks steady now, but the claims-income risk remains real despite more negotiation time.
do: Propose **six-week shorter hours** with unchanged weekly wages, paid teaching and a pre-start written agreement restoring prior hours and wages.
Compare **repair checks** before and during the trial, stopping and using agreed return terms if checks worsen.
Keep **actual repairs** after 2031 unless written changes are agreed, reviewing both household wages monthly.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with more time to negotiate and test rather than rush.
S3.quote: I wouldn't ask the apprentice to hurry unsafe work to rescue an idea I supported.
fieldNote: Her **trial proposal** requires weekly pay, paid teaching and written return terms agreed before starting, not an assumed right to revert.
She treats **collective gains** as something to measure on current work, explicitly denying that a successful trial defeats later robot capability.

steps.text: Propose six-week shorter hours only with unchanged weekly pay and paid required teaching
Require written pre-start agreement restoring previous paid hours and weekly wages if checks worsen
Stop agreed trial if repair checks worsen and invoke written return terms
Keep actual paid repairs after 2031 unless written changes are agreed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives the children room to choose without us naming a safe career at the dinner table. I'd still want workers sharing in any useful gains, rather than prove readiness by working every evening. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still arrive while I expect to need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so retirement isn't something I can assume. Our two current wages and five-month reserve make the next few years manageable, and no cut to my partner's hours is confirmed. The later change is on my mind, but I don't feel our next mortgage payment is threatened in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pursuing the same trial now, starting only with unchanged weekly pay, paid teaching and written return terms if checks got worse. My partner and I would review actual wages and the reserve every six months. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repair work under the actual agreed terms and reopen the staff discussion if hours or tasks changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later years, with enough security now to keep ordinary family plans. I can enjoy an afternoon without pretending the claims desk or my trade will last unchanged. The point of having time is to use some of it for living too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an older family remove the need for those wage checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what support our children will need or what the mortgage balance will be. We'd use the actual household figures at the time. I wouldn't treat somebody finishing school as a replacement income for their parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the employer never agreed a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the paid job and keep making a specific request with colleagues rather than work fewer hours on my own authority. I'd still want to see what changes were actually being introduced. An interesting proposal is not a contract, even after ten years.

say: I'd keep **children's choices** open rather than announce one safe occupation for the family.
I'd seek **shared gains** without treating unpaid evenings as proof of readiness.
think: Our **current wages** and five-month reserve make the next few years manageable, with no confirmed desk-hours cut.
I remain **uneasy** about later change and cannot assume retirement or adult children remove the need for wages.
do: Propose **six-week shorter hours** with unchanged weekly wages, paid teaching and a pre-start written agreement restoring prior hours and wages.
Review **actual wages** and reserve use with my partner every six months.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 under agreed terms and reopen staff discussions if hours or tasks change.
feel: **Uneasy** about later years, with present security sufficient to enjoy ordinary family plans.
S4.quote: An interesting proposal is not a contract, even after ten years.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** changes urgency without assuming protected claims work, a cleared mortgage, pension access or adult children funding their parents.
Her **collective proposal** retains pay, teaching and return conditions; no employer agreement means continuing the actual paid arrangement, not unilateral shorter hours.

steps.text: Propose six-week shorter hours only with unchanged weekly pay and paid required teaching
Require written pre-start agreement restoring previous paid hours and weekly wages if checks worsen
Stop agreed trial if repair checks worsen and invoke written return terms
Keep actual paid repairs after 2036 unless written changes are agreed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a major claims-income loss in 2028, before robots around 2031 could also affect my physical work. Paid required teaching, clear wages and workers involved before staffing decisions would help. I'd also want a way to test sharing the benefit of tools without anybody losing weekly pay for taking part.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether preparing has to mean each household working harder alone. I want a useful tool to give some time back to the people doing the work. I'd rather test that hope honestly than pretend a fairer arrangement already exists.

headlineQuote: I want a useful tool to give some time back to the people doing the work.
portrait: **Nora, 43**, is a highly skilled repair lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence, typical pay and some local alternatives.
Her **partner handles insurance claims**, with two school-age children, a mortgage and five months of expenses saved supporting present household stability.
She uses **AI daily** and tests new tools, while the partner's thinking-work exposure makes household risk differ from her physical repair position.
Her **shorter-hours proposal** preserves weekly pay, paid teaching, written return terms and actual employer agreement rather than assuming shared benefits arrive automatically.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens claims income before robots around 2031 could also reach physical electrical work, risking two close household transitions.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid required teaching** and clear wages would support usable adjustment.
**Worker involvement** and a protected way to test shared gains would help before staffing changes become settled decisions.
